title: Networks of triblock ellipses: from kagome order to disordered porous networks
authors: Susanne Wagner, Gerhard Kahl, Carina Karner
abstract: In colloids, anisotropy in either shape or particle interactions can steer assemblies away from close-packed monolayers and towards more intricate structures. In this study we utilize both shape and interaction anisotropy to stabilize porous surface assemblies of triblock elliptical particles, whose surfaces are decorated with two attractive patches at opposite poles. The resulting structures display a tunable degree of crystalline kagome order, controlled by quenching the temperature and/or changing the chemical potential. In particular, we find evidence that nucleation into the kagome lattice proceeds via a one-step pathway, in contrast to the two-step route widely reported in spherical triblock systems, making triblock ellipses an interesting model system for studying how self-assembly pathways change with particle shape. Beyond ordered crystalline structures, we find disordered porous networks with complex internal geometry. To characterize this range of assemblies, we introduce a particle-patch graph that explicitly captures the localization of bonds at distinct patches. Bonding motifs follow directly from this representation, while the loops, that we identify as the pore boundaries, can be determined from the graph's planar embedding. We detect all loops as the face boundaries in the planar embedding by means of a face-walking algorithm, distinct from shortest-path approaches used in ring detection. Together with a new local and global order parameter measuring the loop network's regularity with respect to a selected loop size, this framework connects microscopic bonding motifs to mesoscopic pore properties and quantifies the tunable order of these porous assemblies.
summary: This paper uses colloidal ellipses with directional patches to study self-assembly, demonstrating that particle shape and interaction anisotropy control the formation of porous networks. By developing a particle-patch graph and using graph theory, the authors quantify the transition from ordered kagome lattices to disordered porous states. This work provides a detailed, quantitative framework for linking microscopic bonding rules to macroscopic network topology.
main_problem: The study investigates how shape and interaction anisotropy dictate the self-assembly pathways and resulting porous structures of colloidal particles.
main_result: The system exhibits tunable crystalline kagome order, and the nucleation into this ordered phase follows a one-step pathway, contrasting with spherical systems.
method: The research employs Monte Carlo simulations combined with advanced graph theory techniques to map microscopic bonding motifs to mesoscopic pore network properties.
model_or_system: The model uses colloidal particles shaped as triblock ellipses, decorated with two attractive patches at opposite poles, allowing for both shape and interaction anisotropy.
key_observables: Kagome lattice order parameter ($\Gamma_6$), loop size distribution, bonding motif concentrations, and the particle-patch graph structure.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the particle aspect ratio ($\kappa=2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the particle-patch graph to correctly distinguish bonds formed at different patches, and loop detection uses a face-walking algorithm.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the kagome lattice unit cell, the comparison between particle and patch graphs, and cross-sections showing the distribution of bonding motifs and loop sizes across different thermodynamic regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and the necessary graph representation (particle-patch graph) to detailing the simulation methods (MC moves, plateau detection) and finally applying these tools to characterize structural transitions, motif formation, and pore network topology.
why_interesting: While focused on classical colloids, the rigorous application of statistical mechanics principles to characterize phase transitions, order parameters, and structural pathways in anisotropic systems provides a strong methodological framework applicable to complex quantum many-body systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) A network of patchy ellipses (elliptic cores in gray, patches in orange) abstracted by (b) the particle graph as well as (c) the particle-patch graph, with a particle represented as a core node (black) connected to its two patch nodes (gray), and a bond represented as an edge connecting two patches; A particle with two neighboring particles connected (d) by one bond per opposing patch and (e) by two bonds at the same patch; (f-g) the associated particle graphs and (h-i) the associated particle-patch graphs; (j-n) typical bonding motifs and their corresponding patch graphs: (j) pair, (k) triangle, (l) open triangle, (m) N-motif and (n) W-motif.
Figure 2: (a) The particle-patch graph and (b) the corresponding cyclic subgraph that represent a network of patchy ellipses forming a nucleus at the early stages of nucleation.
Figure 3: A particle (dark-gray) has at most two adjacent loops (light-gray), which define its local neighborhood for the local loop order parameter in Equ. (1).

Figure 4: State diagram in the plane of chemical potential µ and temperature T. Light blue indicates the gas phase, mid-blue frame indicates nucleating states, all other states enter the production run in an assembled state. Color scale of the nucleating and assembled states denotes the fraction of trajectories that reach an energy plateau within the simulation time, ranging from 0 (orange), where none of the trajectories plateau, to 1 (light gray), where all trajectories do.

Figure 5: Panels (a)-(c): snapshots of configurations at temperature T = 0.145 with chemical potential at (a) µ = −5; (b) µ = −1; (c) µ = 4. Particles are colored according to their loop size: particles in 4-loops (light-green), 5-loops (blue), 6-loops (dark-green), 7-loops (red) and 8-loops (light-green). Particles not in a loop or in a loop of size ≥9 are colored in light-gray. As a particle may belong to up to two loops, we visually resolve this ambiguity by picking the color according to this order: 5-loops, 7-loops, 6-loops, 4-loops, 8-loops.
